source_text: Administrationem corporis sic animo esse commissam, ut fructus operis fieret utrique communis, et vel virtutis exercitae gaudia, vel insolentiae poenas cum eius quam hic non bene rexerat, carnis afflictione sentiret innocentiae
pass_a_gloss: Care of-the-body thus to-the-soul to-be entrusted, so-that/as fruit of-the-work fieret utrique common, and or of-virtue practiced joys, or of-recklessness penalties when/with his/its than/which here not well had-ruled, of-flesh by-suffering sentiret innocentiae.
pass_b_english: The care of the body has been entrusted to the soul in such a way that both share in the fruit of the action: either the joys of practiced virtue, or the penalties for recklessness, together with the suffering of the flesh that the soul failed to govern well here.
At the beginning of life, human nature is rich with the gift of innocence.

choices.why: Image of God in the soul; keep soul not 'mind' or 'life-force'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
